homePage.editorialPara1: The Lake District is England's largest national park. It holds the country's highest mountain, Scafell Pike at 978 metres, and its deepest lake, Wastwater. The National Park Authority counts at least 200 fell tops; Alfred Wainwright wrote about 214 of them, and those 214 are the Wainwrights.
homePage.editorialPara2: The ten highest include Scafell Pike, Scafell, Helvellyn, Skiddaw, Bowfell and Great Gable. Lower fells such as Catbells above Derwentwater make a shorter day.
homePage.editorialPara3: Mountain weather is not valley weather. Before any fell walk, read the mountain forecast from MWIS or the Met Office, carry a map and compass, and know how to use them.
homePage.editorialPara4: This site has heights and grid references for all 214 Wainwrights, route guides for 21 of them, walking circuits of two to four days, and notes on where to stay.
homePage.featureCard1Text: Keswick for the northern fells, Ambleside and Langdale for the central and southern fells, Glenridding and Patterdale for Helvellyn.
homePage.featureCard2Text: Each winter, usually from December, the National Park's Fell Top Assessors walk up Helvellyn and report the conditions on the summit.
homePage.featureCard3Text: Rescue on the fells is run by volunteer teams. In an emergency, dial 999 or 112, ask for Police, then Mountain Rescue.

accommodationPage.pageDesc: Where to base yourself for the fells, area by area, with a few named places to stay and what their own websites say they offer.
accommodationPage.tip1: Book well ahead in summer. Keswick, Ambleside and Glenridding fill weeks ahead. Mid-week is easier than weekends.
accommodationPage.tip2: Ask about boot drying when booking. Good walkers accommodation will have a drying room or boot store.
accommodationPage.tip3: Base yourself according to your fells. Keswick for northern fells, Ambleside for central and southern, Glenridding for Helvellyn.
accommodationPage.tip4: Flexible cancellation matters. Mountain weather is unpredictable. Book refundable rates when possible.

itinerariesPage.howToPlanTitle: How to Plan a Lake District Walking Trip
itinerariesPage.howToPlanPara1: The Lake District is compact enough that a two-day trip can cover two or three fells without difficult logistics. Keswick gives access to Skiddaw, Blencathra and Catbells. Ambleside and Langdale cover the southern and central fells. Glenridding and Patterdale are the base for Helvellyn and the eastern fells.
itinerariesPage.howToPlanPara2: For multi-day trips, base yourself in one area. Keswick has the widest accommodation choice and good transport. Ambleside is central. Glenridding and Buttermere are quieter but more limited. Book accommodation well ahead in summer.
itinerariesPage.howToPlanPara3: The order matters. Don't do Scafell Pike on day one if you're not hill-fit. Build up: start with Catbells or Latrigg, move to Blencathra or Helvellyn, save the big days for when your legs are in. Check the weather each morning.
itinerariesPage.howToPlanPara4: Book accommodation before you arrive. Popular bases fill weeks ahead in summer. Check MWIS and the Met Office mountain forecast each morning. Take a map and compass. Mobile coverage is patchy on the fells.

conditionsPage.pageDesc: The current wind near Grasmere and general notes on popular fells. This page does not report live conditions on the fells: check MWIS and the Met Office before setting out.
conditionsPage.aboutLinksPara1: Mountain weather changes fast. What looks clear from the valley can be clagged in on the summit. Wind strength increases with height. A 15 mph breeze at Grasmere can feel like 30 mph on Helvellyn.
conditionsPage.aboutLinksPara2: Check MWIS (Mountain Weather Information Service) and the Met Office mountain forecast before any walk. In winter, the Lake District National Park's Weatherline service adds a daily report from the summit of Helvellyn. This page is not a substitute for proper planning.
conditionsPage.aboutLinksPara3: Visibility matters as much as wind. Navigation on the fells requires a map and compass when the cloud is down. Clear conditions mean summit views and easier route-finding.
conditionsPage.conditionsDisclaimer: The fell notes on this page are general route notes and are not updated daily. The wind figure is a model reading for one point near Grasmere, not a summit forecast. Always check MWIS and the Met Office before travel. Hike The Lakes accepts no liability for conditions that differ from this page.
